106.title: Sitting between
106.hook: a short sitting between prostrations, asking forgiveness
106.howItsDone: Between the two prostrations of each unit, Muslims sit briefly and still, commonly saying rabbi ighfir li, my Lord, forgive me, or a longer supplication for mercy, guidance, well-being and provision.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sujud, the prostration, forehead on the ground, the closest a person gets. Your line was closest when lowest.

The second after a door shuts. The breath between two sentences in a hard conversation. The red light before it turns green. Small pauses, usually rushed through or filled with a phone. In the prayer, one of these tiny pauses is built in on purpose. The forehead comes up from the floor. The person sits back on their heels, and for a few seconds, before going down again, sits still and says something short. It would be easy to skip. The Prophet ﷺ never did.
screen: `THE SMALLEST PAUSES.` → `UP FROM THE FLOOR.` → `A FEW SECONDS, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The sitting is often called jalsa, just a sitting, from the everyday word for sitting down. Every unit of prayer has two prostrations, and between them the person rises with Allahu akbar and sits, usually on the left foot with the right foot upright, hands resting on the thighs. What do they say? A hadith in the Sunan, from the companion Hudhayfah, reports the Prophet saying here: rabbi ighfir li, rabbi ighfir li. My Lord, forgive me. My Lord, forgive me. That's it. Another report, from Ibn Abbas, gives a longer line, asking God to forgive, to have mercy, to guide, to give well-being, and to provide: five things in one breath. Either one is said quietly, then Allahu akbar, and back down to the floor. Now the surprise. You'd think such a short moment would be hurried. A companion named Anas, in Bukhari, said the Prophet would sit between the two prostrations so long that someone would say, he's forgotten. He hadn't. He was just staying there. The hadith of the man who prayed too fast, met twice already on this path, includes this too: sit until you're at rest in your sitting. So the pause isn't empty space between two important things. It's its own small place. Down to the floor, closest to God; up, sitting, and the first thing said is forgive me; then down again. A rhythm like breathing: low, a breath between, low again.
screen: `JALSA — JUST A SITTING.` · `MY LORD, FORGIVE ME.` · `SO LONG THEY THOUGHT HE'D FORGOTTEN.` · `SIT UNTIL YOU'RE AT REST.` · then, large: `LOW, A BREATH, LOW AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit back, on your heels if that's comfortable, or in a chair with your hands resting on your thighs, and let one breath come in and go out. If you pray, say it once, quietly: rabbi ighfir li, my Lord, forgive me; if you don't, think of one thing you'd like to be let off for, and hold it lightly. Then stay seated, and let the pause be long.
Jalsa. The short sitting between the two prostrations, where the words are: my Lord, forgive me. Today's word.
Your line: a breath between. Even the shortest pause in the prayer has its own words. Day one hundred six.

107.title: The testimony in the sitting
107.hook: the finger raised, the greeting on the Prophet ﷺ and the righteous
107.carry: peace on us and the good
107.howItsDone: After every second unit and at the end of each prayer, Muslims sit and recite the tashahhud, beginning at-tahiyyatu lillah and ending with the testimony of faith, raising the right index finger as they bear witness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jalsa, the short sitting between the prostrations, where the words are my Lord, forgive me. Your line was a breath between.

A companion named Ibn Mas'ud remembered how he learned today's words. Not from a page, and not in passing. The Prophet ﷺ held Ibn Mas'ud's hand between his own two palms, the way a grandparent holds a child's hand to shape a letter, and taught him the words the way he'd teach a chapter of the Qur'an. At the end of every second unit of prayer, and at the very end, the person sits and says them, and near the end, lifts one finger.
screen: `A HAND HELD BETWEEN TWO PALMS.` → `TAUGHT LIKE A SURAH.` → `ONE FINGER RAISED.`

segments.voice: It's called tashahhud, from the root for witnessing, because it ends with the testimony: I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger. As the person says it, the index finger of the right hand is raised, pointing to the one God. The schools differ on exactly when to raise it and whether to move it. But it begins with a greeting, and there's a story in Bukhari about how that came to be. Ibn Mas'ud said that early on, the companions would say in the sitting: peace be on Allah, peace on Jibril, peace on Mika'il, peace on so-and-so. The Prophet turned to them and said: don't say peace be on Allah, for Allah is Himself the Peace. Say instead: at-tahiyyatu lillah, all greetings are for Allah, and the prayers and the good things. Peace be on you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings. Peace be on us and on the righteous servants of Allah. Then he added one more thing: when you say that, it reaches every righteous servant in the heavens and on the earth. Not just friends. Not just one community. Every righteous servant, anywhere. Someone sitting on the floor of one small room sends peace to all of them.
screen: `TASHAHHUD — FROM WITNESSING.` · `DON'T SAY PEACE ON ALLAH.` · `ALL GREETINGS ARE FOR ALLAH.` · `IT REACHES EVERY RIGHTEOUS SERVANT.` · then, large: `PEACE ON US AND THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Sit with your hands resting on your thighs, and say the first line slowly, three times: at-tahiyyatu lillah, all greetings are for Allah. If you pray, you can go on: was-salawatu wat-tayyibat, and the prayers and the good things. If you don't, hold the image of peace going out from where you sit to every good person, everywhere, and keep one of them you know by name in mind.
Tashahhud. The testimony in the sitting: greetings to Allah, peace on the Prophet, on us and on the righteous, then the witness, finger raised. Today's word.
Your line: peace on us and the good. The greeting travels much further than the room. That's day one hundred seven.

108.title: The peace to both sides
108.hook: turn right, then left: peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah
108.howItsDone: Muslims end every prayer by turning the head to the right and then to the left, saying as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah each time, greeting the angels and the worshippers on either side.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tashahhud, the testimony in the sitting, with peace sent to every righteous servant. Your line was peace on us and the good.
screen: `TASHAHHUD — PEACE ON US AND THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: How do you end a phone call with someone you love? Not just click. You say bye, and bye, and okay, bye, love you, bye. Endings matter. They tell the other person how you're leaving. The prayer's door closed behind you at the start, with Allahu akbar. For a few minutes you've been somewhere else: standing, bowing, on the floor, sitting. Now you have to come back into the room. How does the prayer let you walk back out?
screen: `OKAY, BYE, LOVE YOU, BYE.` → `ENDINGS MATTER.` → `HOW DO YOU WALK BACK OUT?`

segments.voice: The ending is called taslim, from the same root as salaam, the very first word on this path. In the most common form, at the end of the last sitting, the person turns the head to the right and says: as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah. Then to the left, and again. Remember the hadith from day one hundred one: the prayer's opening is the takbir, and its closing is the taslim. The door that closed with Allahu akbar opens again with peace. Who is the greeting for? Scholars give a few answers: the angels, whom the tradition places on the right and left of every person; the people praying beside you in the line; Muslims everywhere. The words are plural, you all, so there's room for all of them. A small story in Sahih Muslim shows how ordinary it's meant to be. A companion named Jabir said that when they prayed with the Prophet ﷺ, they used to wave their hands at the salam, to one side and the other. The Prophet asked why they were waving like restless horses flicking their tails, and said it was enough to rest the hand on the thigh and greet your brother on your right and on your left. So the prayer doesn't end with a request, or a flourish. It ends with you looking at the people beside you and wishing them peace and mercy.
screen: `TASLIM — FROM THE ROOT OF SALAAM.` · `RIGHT, THEN LEFT.` · `ITS CLOSING IS THE TASLIM.` · `NO NEED TO WAVE.` · then, large: `PEACE TO THE PERSON BESIDE YOU.`

segments.voice: Sit with your hands on your thighs and turn your head slowly to the right; if you pray, say as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah, and if not, wish well whoever is on that side of you, in the next room, the next house, the next city. Then turn slowly to the left and do the same, and come back to center.
Taslim. The closing of the prayer: peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah, turning right, then left. Today's word.
Your line: peace, both ways. Even the way out of the prayer is a greeting. See you tomorrow.

109.title: Counting the units
109.hook: two at dawn, four, four, three at sunset, four at night
109.howItsDone: Muslims pray seventeen obligatory rak'ahs a day: two at fajr, four at dhuhr, four at asr, three at maghrib and four at isha, and travelers commonly shorten the four-rak'ah prayers to two.

segments.voice: Yesterday: taslim, the closing, peace to the right, then the left. Your line was peace, both ways.

Some things you learn as a rhythm before you learn them as facts. Thirty days has September. A phone number sung in an old commercial. The daily prayers can be learned the same way, as a string of numbers said in one breath: two, four, four, three, four. It sounds like a code. It's actually a map of the whole day, and each number counts one thing: a unit of the prayer. You've learned every piece of it this week. Today, how the pieces add up.
screen: `THIRTY DAYS HAS SEPTEMBER.` → `TWO, FOUR, FOUR, THREE, FOUR.` → `A MAP OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The unit is called a rak'ah, from the same root as ruku', the bow. One rak'ah is one full cycle: standing and reciting, the bow, rising, two prostrations with the sitting between. The pieces from this past week, in order, make one rak'ah, and the daily prayers are built out of them. Fajr, at dawn: two. Dhuhr, midday: four. Asr, afternoon: four. Maghrib, sunset: three. Isha, night: four. Seventeen in all, every day. After every second rak'ah the person sits for the tashahhud, and in the last one adds the taslim, so a four-rak'ah prayer has a sitting in the middle and one at the end. Why these numbers? The tradition keeps them because this is how the Prophet ﷺ prayed. But there's a story in them. Aisha, his wife, said in a hadith in Bukhari that the prayer was first made obligatory as two rak'ahs each. Then the traveler's prayer was left at two, and the prayer at home was increased. That's why, to this day, a traveler shortens the fours to two. The Qur'an gives the permission, in Surah an-Nisa: no sin in shortening the prayer on a journey. The dawn prayer stays two; the sunset prayer stays three. So the numbers carry a little history: two was the original shape, the day's middle prayers grew, and on the road the fours go back to two.

segments.voice: Hold up your hand and count it through: thumb, fajr, two; index finger, dhuhr, four; middle finger, asr, four; ring finger, maghrib, three; little finger, isha, four. Then say just the numbers, two, four, four, three, four, let your hand rest, and picture one whole rak'ah, from standing to the second prostration, slowly. If you pray, you'll know where you'll be at the next one.
Rak'ah. One unit of prayer, from standing to the second prostration; seventeen of them every day. Today's word.
Your line: two, four, four, three, four. Seventeen units, the whole day in one breath. Day one hundred nine, done.

110.title: Different hands, same prayer
110.hook: schools differ on hand placement and small details, and all are valid within the tradition
110.howItsDone: A Muslim usually prays according to one school of law, often the one of their family or region, and pray side by side in the mosque with people who hold their hands, say amin or raise their hands a little differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rak'ah, one full unit of prayer, seventeen a day. Your line was two, four, four, three, four.

Stand at the back of a big mosque during Friday prayer and look down the line. The man on the left has his hands folded low, below the navel. The one next to him, higher, on the chest. The one next to him has his arms hanging straight at his sides. At the end of the Fatiha, some say amin out loud; some whisper it. A newcomer might think half the room is doing it wrong. Nobody in the line thinks so. They're shoulder to shoulder, and they bow at the same moment.
screen: `HANDS LOW, HANDS HIGH, ARMS DOWN.` → `AMIN ALOUD, AMIN WHISPERED.` → `THEY BOW AT THE SAME MOMENT.`

segments.voice: The word is madhhab, a school of law. Literally it means a way of going, the road someone takes. In Islam's first centuries, scholars in different cities worked out how to follow the Qur'an and the Prophet's ﷺ example in daily life, and the ones whose methods lasted became schools. Among Sunni Muslims there are four, each named after a scholar: Abu Hanifa in Iraq, Malik in Medina, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Twelver Shia Muslims follow the Ja'fari school, named after Ja'far al-Sadiq. Why differ on something as simple as hands? Because the reports differ. Companions saw the Prophet pray over years, in different places, and remembered different details. So the Hanafi school commonly teaches hands folded below the navel; the Shafi'i, above the navel, below the chest; the Maliki school is known for leaving the arms at the sides, and so is Ja'fari practice. Each has its reasons, going back to a report. There's a well-known story about Imam Malik. A caliph, the story goes, wanted to make Malik's book, the Muwatta, the law for the whole empire. Malik said no. The companions, he said, had spread out to different lands, and each land had its own knowledge from them. Leave people with what they have. People sometimes quote a saying, the differing of my community is a mercy; scholars note it isn't a reliable hadith. But the attitude holds: within the tradition, all four Sunni schools are considered valid, and a Muslim can pray behind someone of another school. The details differ. The prayer is one.
screen: `MADHHAB — A WAY OF GOING.` · `FOUR SUNNI SCHOOLS, AND THE JA'FARI.` · `THE REPORTS DIFFER.` · `MALIK SAID: LEAVE PEOPLE BE.` · then, large: `THE DETAILS DIFFER. THE PRAYER IS ONE.`

segments.voice: Picture the line in that mosque, or watch a short video of a prayer, and look at the hands: low, high, at the sides. If something in you wants to decide who's right, let it go. Then stand and try each for one breath, hands low, hands high, arms hanging, and notice the prayer doesn't change; if you pray, you already know your own way, so just hold it gently.
Madhhab. A school of Islamic law, a way of going; four Sunni schools and the Ja'fari, one prayer. Today's word.
Your line: many hands, one prayer. Shoulder to shoulder, the line still bows together. That's one hundred ten.

111.title: When you can't stand
111.hook: you pray sitting, lying, or by signs; the prayer bends to the body
111.howItsDone: Muslims who can't stand pray sitting, often on a chair, leaning forward for the bow and a little further for the prostration; those who can't sit pray lying on their side or back, using signs with the head or eyes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: madhhab, the schools of law, hands low, high or at the sides. Your line was many hands, one prayer.

Walk into almost any mosque today and look along the back wall. There's a row of plastic chairs. An older man sits in one, and when the line bows, he leans forward from his seat. When they go down to the floor, he leans a little further. Nobody looks twice. Across town, in a hospital bed, a woman who can't sit up at all moves her eyes and her lips through the same prayer. For ten days now, this path has followed the body as it stands, bows and falls to the ground. So what happens when the body can't?
screen: `A ROW OF CHAIRS AT THE BACK.` → `A HOSPITAL BED.` → `WHEN THE BODY CAN'T.`

segments.voice: A short hadith in Bukhari answers it. A companion named Imran ibn Husayn had a painful illness and asked the Prophet ﷺ how to pray. The answer was three lines. Pray standing. If you can't, then sitting. If you can't, then on your side. Scholars filled in the rest: if you can't bow or prostrate, you make the movements with signs, leaning or nodding, a little lower for the prostration than for the bow. If you can't move at all, with your eyes, or in your heart. The prayer keeps going; it just gets smaller to fit. The Prophet himself did this. When he fell from a horse and hurt his side, he prayed sitting, and in his last illness he prayed sitting, too. Underneath is one of the best-known lines in the Qur'an, from the end of Surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's words: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." Scope: what it can hold. The prayer is an obligation, and one that bends to the person. So is the washing, which becomes tayammum without water, and the four rak'ahs that become two on a journey, and, as you'll see, the fast. The prayer isn't only for the strong, the flexible, the young. The man in the plastic chair isn't praying a lesser prayer. In the tradition, he's doing exactly what's asked of him. The prayer fits him.
screen: `STANDING. SITTING. ON YOUR SIDE.` · `BY SIGNS, OR WITH THE EYES.` · `THE PROPHET PRAYED SITTING TOO.` · `NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE.` · then, large: `THE PRAYER FITS THE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Stay in your chair: raise your hands for the opening, rest them, and sit tall for the standing. Lean forward from the hips for the bow, come back up, then lean a little further for each prostration, lower than the bow, sitting back between, slowly, the way someone moves when this is what the body allows. If you pray, you can say the words as you go.
Tayammum, the dry washing used when there's no water, one more way the prayer bends to the body: sitting if you can't stand, on your side if you can't sit, by signs if you can't move.
Your line: the prayer fits you. It steps down to meet the body it has. See you tomorrow.

112.title: One whole prayer
112.hook: putting it together: dawn prayer, two units, start to finish
112.tomorrow: When you stop, and start again
112.howItsDone: The dawn prayer, fajr, is two rak'ahs prayed between first light and sunrise, recited aloud when leading, and it is preceded by two voluntary rak'ahs, often prayed at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tayammum, and how the prayer bends to the body: sitting, on your side, or by signs. Your line was the prayer fits you.

It's like learning a song one bar at a time. Fifteen bars, one a day: the intention, cleanness, a direction, five times, two words that open the door, the standing, the bow, the rising, the prostration, the sitting between, the testimony, the peace to both sides, the count, the schools, and the chair at the back. Today you hear it played through, once, from the first note to the last. The shortest of the five: dawn, two units. Today: fajr.
screen: `FIFTEEN PIECES, ONE A DAY.` → `ONE BAR AT A TIME.` → `NOW PLAYED THROUGH.`

segments.voice: It's still dark. The sky is only beginning to gray. That's fajr's time. The person has made wudu, is on a clean spot, facing the qiblah. In the heart, the intention: two rak'ahs of the dawn prayer. Hands rise. Allahu akbar. The door closes behind. Hands fold, eyes down. The Fatiha, then a short surah, recited aloud if leading, because the dawn prayer is one of the spoken ones. Allahu akbar, and the bow: glory to my Lord the Great, three times, settled. Rising: Allah hears whoever praises Him. Our Lord, and to You be the praise. Allahu akbar, and down: forehead, nose, hands, knees, toes. Glory to my Lord the Most High. Up to sit: my Lord, forgive me. Down again, the second prostration. That's one rak'ah. Allahu akbar, up to stand, and the cycle repeats: Fatiha, a surah, bow, rise, prostrate, sit, prostrate. Then, instead of standing, the person stays seated for the tashahhud: all greetings are for Allah, peace on the Prophet ﷺ, peace on us and the righteous, finger raised for the witness. Then blessings on the Prophet and on Ibrahim. Then right: as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah. Left: the same. And it's over. Five minutes, maybe less. Before it come two voluntary rak'ahs, which the Prophet said, in Sahih Muslim, are better than the world and everything in it. Every piece you've learned, in order, before the sun is up.
screen: `STILL DARK. WUDU. FACING THE QIBLAH.` · `STAND, BOW, RISE, PROSTRATE, SIT.` · `ONCE MORE, THEN THE TESTIMONY.` · `PEACE, RIGHT AND LEFT.` · then, large: `EVERY PIECE, IN ORDER, BEFORE SUNRISE.`

segments.voice: If you pray, pray the two rak'ahs now, slowly, the way you've learned them, noticing each piece as it passes. If you don't, walk through the shape without words, standing or in your chair: raise your hands, stand, bow, rise, go down or lean, sit, go down again; then once more, then sit, and turn your head right, and left.
Fajr, the two-unit dawn prayer: takbir to taslim, every piece in order, the whole thing played through for the first time.
Your line: the whole thing. Tomorrow: what happens when you stop. Two weeks of prayer, done.
